chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter V
paragraphs: That same evening, a heated argument broke out among the officers in Denisov's quarters.

"I'm telling you, Rostov, you have to apologize to the colonel!" said a tall, gray-haired staff captain with an enormous mustache and deeply lined face, addressing Rostov, who was flushed red with emotion.
The staff captain, Kirsten, had been demoted to the ranks twice over matters of honor, and twice had won back his commission.

"I won't let anyone call me a liar!" Rostov burst out. "He said I was lying, and I told him he was lying. And that's where it stands. He can put me on duty every day or throw me in the brig, but nobody can force me to apologize. If he, as regimental commander, considers it beneath his dignity to give me satisfaction, then—"

"Just hold on a moment, my dear fellow, and listen," the staff captain interrupted in his deep bass voice, calmly stroking his long mustache. "You told the colonel, in front of other officers, that one of the officers had stolen—"

"It's not my fault the conversation started in front of other officers. Maybe I shouldn't have spoken in front of them, but I'm no diplomat. That's exactly why I joined the hussars—because I thought here you wouldn't need to play games. And then he tells me I'm lying, so let him give me satisfaction—"
"That's all well and good. Nobody thinks you're a coward, but that's beside the point. Ask Denisov whether it's even possible for a cadet to demand satisfaction from his regimental commander."
Denisov sat gloomily chewing his mustache, listening to the conversation with obvious reluctance to get involved. He answered the staff captain's question with a disapproving shake of his head.
"You brought up this ugly business in front of other officers," the staff captain continued, "and Bogdanich"—that was the colonel's nickname—"shut you down."
"He didn't shut me down. He said I was telling an untruth."
"Fine, have it your way. You said a lot of foolish things to him, and now you need to apologize."
"Absolutely not!" Rostov exclaimed.

"I didn't expect this from you," said the staff captain, his tone now serious and stern. "You refuse to apologize, but it's not just about him—it's about the whole regiment. All of us. You're in the wrong on every count. Here's the thing: you should have thought it through and asked for advice. But no, you went and blurted the whole thing out right in front of the officers. What was the colonel supposed to do? Have the officer court-martialed and disgrace the entire regiment? Disgrace all of us because of one scoundrel? Is that really how you see it? We don't see it that way. Bogdanich did the right thing—he told you that what you were saying wasn't true. It's not pleasant, but what else could he do, my dear fellow? You brought this on yourself. And now some kind of pride won't let you apologize, and you want to make the whole thing public. You're offended about extra duty, but why can't you apologize to an old and honorable officer? Whatever else you might think of Bogdanich, he's an honorable and brave old colonel! You're quick to take offense, but you don't mind dragging the whole regiment through the mud!" The staff captain's voice began to shake. "You've barely been with the regiment, my boy. You're here today and tomorrow you'll be posted somewhere as an adjutant, and you'll be able to shrug it off when people say, 'There are thieves among the Pavlograd officers!' But it's not the same for us! Am I right, Denisov? It's not the same!"
Denisov stayed silent and motionless, only occasionally glancing at Rostov with his glittering black eyes.

"You're too proud to apologize," the staff captain went on, "but we old fellows who've grown up in this regiment and, God willing, are going to die in it—we care about the regiment's honor. Bogdanich knows that. Yes, we care about it, old fellow! And all this isn't right—it just isn't right! You can be offended or not, but I always say what's true. It isn't right!"
The staff captain stood up and turned away from Rostov.
"That's twue, damn it all!" Denisov shouted, jumping to his feet. "Come on, Wostov, come on!"
Rostov, turning red and pale by turns, looked from one officer to the other.

"No, gentlemen, no... don't think... I understand completely. You're wrong to think that of me... I... for me... for the honor of the regiment I'd... Well, I'll prove it in battle. For me, the honor of the regiment... Well, never mind—it's true, I'm in the wrong. Completely in the wrong. So what else do you want?..."
"Now that's the spirit, Count!" the staff captain cried, turning back around and clapping Rostov on the shoulder with his big hand.
"I tell you," Denisov shouted, "he's a fine fellow!"
"That's more like it, Count," said the staff captain, now using Rostov's title as if to acknowledge his admission of fault. "Go and apologize, your excellency. Yes, go!"

"Gentlemen, I'll do anything. No one will hear another word from me," Rostov said in a pleading voice, "but I can't apologize—by God, I can't! Do whatever you want with me! How can I go and apologize like a little boy begging for forgiveness?"
Denisov started laughing.
"It'll be worse for you. Bogdanich holds grudges, and you'll pay for your stubbornness," said Kirsten.
"No, I swear it's not stubbornness! I can't explain the feeling. I just can't..."
"Well, suit yourself," said the staff captain. "And what's become of that scoundrel?" he asked Denisov.
"He's weported himself sick. He'll be stwuck off the list tomowwow," Denisov muttered.
"It's an illness—there's no other way to explain it," said the staff captain.
"Illness or not, he'd better not cwoss my path. I'd kill him!" Denisov shouted in a murderous tone.
Just then Zherkov walked into the room.
"What brings you here?" the officers called out, turning to the newcomer.
"We're going into action, gentlemen! Mack has surrendered with his entire army."
"That can't be true!"
"I've seen him with my own eyes!"
"What? You saw the actual Mack? With hands and feet and everything?"
"Into action! Into action! Someone get him a bottle for news like that! But how did you end up here?"

"I've been sent back to the regiment, all because of that devil Mack. An Austrian general complained about me. I congratulated him on Mack's arrival... What's the matter, Rostov? You look like you just stepped out of a steam bath."
"Oh, my dear fellow, we've been in such turmoil here the past two days."
The regimental adjutant came in and confirmed Zherkov's news. They had orders to advance the next day.
"We're going into action, gentlemen!"
"Thank God for that! We've been sitting around here far too long!"

chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter VI
paragraphs: Kutuzov fell back toward Vienna, destroying the bridges over the River Inn at Braunau and the River Traun near Linz as he went. On October 23, the Russian troops were crossing the River Enns. By midday, the Russian baggage train, artillery, and columns of troops were filing through the town of Enns on both sides of the bridge.

It was a warm, rainy autumn day. The wide landscape that opened out below the heights where the Russian batteries guarded the bridge was sometimes veiled by a sheer curtain of slanting rain, and then suddenly revealed in sunlight, with far-off objects glittering as if freshly varnished. Down below, the little town could be seen with its white, red-roofed houses, its cathedral, and its bridge, on both sides of which masses of Russian troops were streaming and jostling. At the bend of the Danube, boats, an island, and a castle with a park stood visible, surrounded by the waters where the Enns flowed into the Danube. The rocky left bank of the Danube was covered with pine forests, with a mysterious backdrop of green treetops and bluish ravines. The towers of a convent rose beyond a stretch of untouched pine forest, and far away on the other side of the Enns, enemy cavalry patrols could be spotted.

On the brow of the hill, among the field guns, the general commanding the rearguard stood with a staff officer, scanning the countryside through his field glass. A little behind them sat Nesvitski, who had been sent to the rearguard by the commander in chief, perched on the trail of a gun carriage. A Cossack who accompanied him had handed over a knapsack and flask, and Nesvitski was treating some officers to pies and genuine doppelkümmel liqueur. The officers had gathered around him gladly, some on their knees, others squatting cross-legged on the wet grass.
"Yes, the Austrian prince who built that castle was no fool. Lovely place! Why aren't you eating, gentlemen?" Nesvitski was saying.

"Thank you very much, Prince," answered one of the officers, pleased to be chatting with such an important staff officer. "It really is a lovely place! We passed right by the park and spotted two deer... and what a magnificent house!"

"Look, Prince," said another officer, who would have loved to take another pie but felt too self-conscious and so pretended to be studying the landscape. "See—our infantry have already made it over there. Look, in the meadow behind the village, three of them are dragging something. They'll clean out that castle," he observed with obvious approval.
"I'm sure they will," said Nesvitski. "No, but what I'd really love," he added, munching a pie with his moist-lipped, handsome mouth, "would be to slip in over there."
He pointed with a grin toward a turreted convent, his eyes narrowing and gleaming.
"Now that would be something, gentlemen!"
The officers laughed.
"Just to ruffle the nuns a bit. I hear there are Italian girls among them. I swear I'd give five years of my life for it!"
"They must be pretty bored too," said one of the bolder officers with a laugh.
Meanwhile, the staff officer up front pointed something out to the general, who looked through his field glass.

"Yes, that's right, that's right," the general said irritably, lowering his field glass and shrugging. "That's right! They'll come under fire at the crossing. And why are they dragging their feet over there?"

On the far side, the enemy was visible to the naked eye, and a milky-white cloud of smoke rose from their battery. Then came the distant boom of a shot, and the Russian troops could be seen rushing toward the crossing.
Nesvitski heaved himself up, puffing, and walked over to the general with a smile.
"Wouldn't your excellency care for a little refreshment?" he offered.
"It's a bad business," the general replied without acknowledging the offer. "Our men have wasted too much time."
"Shall I ride over there, your excellency?" Nesvitski asked.

"Yes, please do," the general answered, and repeated the detailed order that had already been given once before: "And tell the hussars they are to cross last and set fire to the bridge, as I ordered. And the inflammable material on the bridge needs to be inspected again."
"Very good," Nesvitski replied.
He called over the Cossack with his horse, told him to stow the knapsack and flask, and swung his heavy frame easily into the saddle.
"I really will stop by the convent," he told the officers, who watched him with smiles, and he rode off down the winding path along the hillside.
"Now then, Captain, let's see how far it'll carry. Give it a try!" said the general, turning to an artillery officer. "A bit of fun to pass the time."
"Crew, to your guns!" the officer commanded.
In a moment the men came running cheerfully from their campfires and began loading.
"Fire!" came the command.

Number one jumped nimbly aside. The gun roared with a deafening metallic blast, and a whistling shell flew over the heads of the troops below the hill before landing well short of the enemy, a small puff of smoke marking where it burst.

The faces of officers and soldiers alike brightened at the sound. Everyone stood up and began watching the movements of the Russian troops below—as clearly visible as if they were only a stone's throw away—and the approaching enemy further off. At that same moment, the sun broke fully through the clouds, and the sharp crack of the solitary shot merged with the brilliance of the bright sunshine into one joyful, exhilarating impression.

chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter VII
paragraphs: Two enemy shells had already flown across the bridge, where a crush of men was building up. Halfway across, Prince Nesvitski had dismounted and now found his bulky body jammed against the railings. He glanced back, laughing, at the Cossack standing a few steps behind him holding two horses by their bridles. Every time Nesvitski tried to push forward, soldiers and carts shoved him back against the railings, and all he could do was smile.

"Some friend you are!" the Cossack said to a supply wagon driver who was pressing into the infantrymen crowded around his wheels and horses. "What kind of fellow are you? Can't you wait a moment? Don't you see the general needs to get through?"

But the wagon driver paid no attention to the word "general" and shouted at the soldiers blocking his way. "Hey, boys! Keep to the left! Hold up!" But the soldiers, packed shoulder to shoulder with bayonets interlocking, moved across the bridge in a solid mass. Looking over the railing, Prince Nesvitski watched the quick, noisy little waves of the Enns rippling and swirling around the bridge pilings, chasing one another downstream. Looking at the bridge itself, he saw an equally unbroken living wave of soldiers—shoulder straps, covered shakos, knapsacks, bayonets, long muskets, and beneath the shakos, faces with broad cheekbones, hollow cheeks, and dull, tired expressions—and feet trudging through the sticky mud that coated the bridge planks. Sometimes, through this monotonous stream of men, like a fleck of white foam on the river's current, an officer in a cloak, with a face of a different type, squeezed his way through. Sometimes, like a wood chip spinning in the water, a dismounted hussar, an orderly, or a civilian was carried along in the flood of infantry. And sometimes, like a log drifting downstream, an officers' or company baggage wagon—piled high, covered in leather, and hemmed in on every side—rolled across the bridge.
"It's like a dam burst," said the Cossack, giving up hope. "Are there many more of you coming?"
"A million, all but one!" a wisecracking soldier in a torn coat called back with a wink, and passed on, followed by another—an old man.
"If he"—meaning the enemy—"starts firing at the bridge now," the old soldier said glumly to a comrade, "you'll forget all about scratching yourself."
That soldier moved on, and after him came another riding on a cart.
"Where the hell have the leg wrappings been shoved?" an orderly shouted, running behind the cart and rummaging in the back of it.
He too passed on with the wagon. Then came a group of soldiers who had clearly been drinking.
"And then, old fellow, he smacks him right in the teeth with the butt of his rifle..." a soldier with his greatcoat tucked up tight was saying cheerfully, swinging his arm wide.
"Yeah, and that ham was delicious..." another replied with a loud laugh. And they too moved on, so that Nesvitski never learned who had been hit in the teeth, or what ham had to do with any of it.
"Bah! Look at them scurry. One cannonball and they think they're all going to die," a sergeant was saying angrily and reproachfully.

"When it flies past me, Papa—the ball, I mean," said a young soldier with an enormous mouth, barely holding back his laughter. "I felt like I was going to die of fright. I really did, honest to God, I was that scared!" he said, as if boasting about having been frightened.

He too passed on. Then came a cart unlike any of the others. It was a German cart pulled by a pair of horses and led by a German, loaded with what looked like an entire household's belongings. A fine brindled cow with a large udder was tied to the back. A woman carrying an infant, an old woman, and a healthy German girl with bright red cheeks sat perched on feather beds. These refugees had evidently been allowed through by special permission. Every soldier's eyes turned toward the women, and as the cart crawled past at walking pace, every remark the soldiers made was about the two younger ones. Each face wore almost the same grin, reflecting thoughts that were anything but proper.
"Look at that—even the German sausage is clearing out!"
"How about selling me the missus?" another soldier called to the German, who strode along angrily and nervously with his eyes fixed on the ground.
"Look how she's dressed herself up! The devils!"
"Hey, Fedotov—they should quarter you with them!"
"I've seen plenty of that before, mate!"
"Where are you headed?" asked an infantry officer who was eating an apple, also half smiling as he looked at the pretty girl.
The German closed his eyes, indicating he didn't understand.
"Here, take this if you'd like," said the officer, holding out the apple to the girl.

The girl smiled and took it. Nesvitski, like every other man on the bridge, kept his eyes on the women until they had passed. When they were gone, the same stream of soldiers continued with the same kind of chatter, and finally everyone came to a halt. As so often happens, the horses pulling a supply wagon had balked at the end of the bridge, and the entire crowd was forced to wait.

"Why have they stopped? No order at all!" the soldiers grumbled. "Where do you think you're shoving? To hell with you! Can't you wait? It'll be even worse if he sets fire to the bridge. Look—there's an officer stuck too." Different voices in the crowd said these things as the men looked at one another and all pressed toward the far end of the bridge.
Looking down at the waters of the Enns beneath the bridge, Nesvitski suddenly heard a new sound—something approaching fast, something large that splashed into the water.
"See where that one landed!" a soldier nearby said grimly, glancing around at the sound.
"Encouraging us to move faster," said another nervously.
The crowd surged forward again. Nesvitski realized it had been a cannonball.
"Hey, Cossack! My horse!" he called. "Now then, make way! Get out of the way!"

With enormous difficulty he reached his horse, and shouting nonstop, he pushed forward. The soldiers squeezed aside to let him through but immediately pressed in on him again, jamming his leg. Those nearest him weren't to blame—they were being crushed from behind even harder.
"Nesvitski! Nesvitski, you blockhead!" came a hoarse voice from behind.

Nesvitski turned and saw, about fifteen paces back but cut off by the solid, moving mass of infantry, Vaska Denisov—red-faced and shaggy, his cap shoved to the back of his black head, a cloak thrown dashingly over one shoulder.

"Tell these devils—these fiends—to let me through!" Denisov shouted, clearly in a fury, his coal-black eyes with their bloodshot whites glittering and rolling as he waved his sheathed saber in a small, bare hand as red as his face.
"Vaska!" Nesvitski called back joyfully. "What's going on?"

"The squadwon can't get thwough!" Vaska Denisov shouted, baring his white teeth fiercely and spurring his black thoroughbred Arab, which flicked its ears as bayonets grazed it and snorted, spraying white foam from its bit, stamping the bridge planks with its hooves—looking ready to vault right over the railings if its rider allowed it. "What is this? They're like sheep! Just like sheep! Out of the way! Let us through! You there with the cart—I'll cut you down with my saber!" he yelled, actually drawing his saber and brandishing it.
The soldiers crushed against each other with terrified faces, and Denisov managed to reach Nesvitski.
"How is it you're not drunk today?" Nesvitski asked when Denisov had ridden up alongside.
"They don't even give you time to dwink!" Denisov answered. "They keep dwagging the wegiment back and forth all day. If we're going to fight, then let's fight. But God only knows what this is."
"What a dandy you look today!" said Nesvitski, eyeing Denisov's new cloak and saddle cloth.
Denisov grinned, pulled a handkerchief from his sabretache that gave off a waft of perfume, and pressed it to Nesvitski's nose.
"Of course! I'm going into action! I've shaved, bwushed my teeth, and put on cologne."

The imposing bulk of Nesvitski, trailed by his Cossack, combined with Denisov's fierce determination as he swung his sword and shouted like a madman, had such an effect that they managed to force their way through to the far side of the bridge and halt the infantry. At the bridgehead, Nesvitski found the colonel he needed to deliver the order to, and having done so, rode back.

Having cleared the way, Denisov stopped at the end of the bridge. Casually reining in his stallion—which was neighing and pawing the ground, eager to rejoin the other horses—he watched his squadron approaching. The clang of hooves, as if several horses were galloping at once, rang out on the bridge planks, and the squadron, officers in front and men four abreast, spread across the bridge and began emerging on his side.

The infantry soldiers who had been held up stood in the trampled mud near the bridge and watched with that particular mixture of hostility, detachment, and mockery that troops of different branches typically feel when they encounter one another—watching the clean, smart hussars ride past in neat formation.
"Pretty boys! Only good for a parade!" one said.
"What use are they? Just marched around for show!" another remarked.
"Don't kick up the dust, you foot-sloggers!" joked a hussar whose prancing horse had splattered mud on several infantrymen.

"I'd like to see you after a two-day march with a knapsack! Those fancy trousers would get worn through soon enough," said an infantryman, wiping mud off his face with his sleeve. "Sitting up there, you look more like a bird than a man."
"Hey, Zikin, they ought to put you on a horse. You'd be a sight!" said a corporal, teasing a scrawny little soldier bowed under the weight of his knapsack.
"Stick a branch between your legs—that'll do for your horse!" the hussar shouted back.

chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter VIII
paragraphs: The last of the infantry hurried across the bridge, bunching tighter as they neared it, as if squeezing through a funnel. Finally all the baggage wagons had crossed, the crowding eased, and the last battalion reached the bridge. Now only Denisov's squadron of hussars remained on the far side, facing the enemy. The French could be seen from the hill on the opposite bank but were not yet visible from the bridge itself, because the horizon as viewed from the river valley was formed by rising ground barely half a mile away. At the foot of the hill stretched wasteland where a few groups of Cossack scouts were moving about. Then suddenly, on the road at the top of the high ground, artillery and troops in blue uniforms appeared. These were the French. A group of Cossack scouts trotted back down the hill. All the officers and men of Denisov's squadron tried to talk about other things and look elsewhere, but every one of them was thinking only about what was up on that hilltop, and they kept glancing at the shapes appearing on the skyline—shapes they knew to be enemy troops. The weather had cleared again since midday, and the sun was sinking brightly over the Danube and the dark hills surrounding it. It was quiet, and at intervals the sound of bugle calls and shouting from the enemy drifted down from the hill. Between the squadron and the enemy there was now nothing but a handful of scattered skirmishers. An empty stretch of about seven hundred yards was all that separated them. The enemy had stopped firing, and that stern, menacing, untouchable line dividing two hostile armies could be felt more sharply than ever.

One step beyond that invisible boundary—which feels like the line between the living and the dead—lies uncertainty, suffering, and death. And what is over there? Who is over there? Beyond that field, that tree, that sunlit rooftop? No one knows, but you want to know. You are afraid to cross that line, and yet you long to cross it, knowing that sooner or later you must, and that you will have to discover what lies on the other side—just as you will inevitably have to learn what lies beyond death. But you are strong, healthy, cheerful, and keyed up, surrounded by others who are just as excited and alive. That is what anyone thinks, or at least feels, when they come within sight of the enemy, and that feeling lends a special intensity and joyful sharpness to everything that happens in such moments.

On the high ground where the enemy stood, a puff of cannon smoke rose and a ball came whistling over the heads of the hussar squadron. The officers who had been clustered together rode off to their positions. The hussars carefully straightened their formation. Silence fell over the entire squadron. Every man watched the enemy ahead and the squadron commander, waiting for the order. A second cannonball flew past, then a third. They were clearly aiming at the hussars, but each ball whistled rapidly overhead and landed somewhere beyond. The hussars didn't turn around, but at the sound of each shot—as if on command—the whole squadron, with its rows of faces so alike and yet so different, rose slightly in the stirrups, held its breath while the ball passed, and then settled back. Without turning their heads, the soldiers stole glances at each other, curious to read their comrades' reactions. On every face, from Denisov's down to the bugler's, the same expression showed around the chin and mouth: a mixture of tension, irritation, and excitement. The quartermaster glared at his men as though threatening punishment. Cadet Mironov flinched every time a ball flew past. Rostov, on the left flank astride his horse Rook—a handsome animal despite its lame leg—wore the happy look of a schoolboy called up for an exam before a large audience, confident he's going to shine. He kept glancing around with a bright, clear expression, as if inviting everyone to notice how calm he was under fire. But despite himself, that same hint of something new and serious showed around his mouth too.
"Who's ducking over there? Cadet Miwonov! That's not wight! Look at me!" Denisov called out. Unable to stay still, he kept wheeling his horse back and forth in front of the squadron.

The black, hairy, snub-nosed face of Vaska Denisov, and his whole short, sturdy frame with its sinewy hand and stubby fingers gripping the hilt of his bared saber, looked just as it always did—especially toward evening when he'd emptied his second bottle. He was only redder than usual. With his shaggy head thrown back the way birds do when they drink, pressing his spurs ruthlessly into the flanks of his good horse Bedouin, sitting as if he were falling backward in the saddle, he galloped to the other end of the squadron and shouted in a hoarse voice for the men to check their pistols. Then he rode up to Kirsten. The staff captain, on his broad-backed, steady mare, came toward him at a walk. His face with its long mustache was as serious as ever; only his eyes were brighter than usual.
"Well, what do you think?" Kirsten said to Denisov. "It won't come to a fight. Watch—we'll pull back."
"The devil only knows what they're up to!" Denisov muttered. "Ah, Wostov!" he cried, catching sight of the cadet's bright face. "You've finally got your chance!"
He smiled approvingly, clearly pleased with the young man. Rostov felt completely happy. Just then the commander appeared on the bridge. Denisov galloped up to him.
"Your excellency! Let us attack them! I'll dwive them off!"

"Attack, indeed!" the colonel said in a bored voice, scrunching his face as though swatting away a fly. "And why are you standing here? Can't you see the skirmishers are pulling back? Lead the squadron out."

The squadron crossed the bridge and moved out of range without losing a single man. The second squadron, which had been in the front line, followed them across, and the last Cossacks withdrew from the far bank.

The two Pavlograd squadrons, having crossed the bridge, retired up the hill one after the other. Their colonel, Karl Bogdanich Schubert, rode up to Denisov's squadron and proceeded at a walking pace near Rostov, without taking any notice of him—even though this was their first encounter since the incident with Telyanin. Rostov, feeling that he was at the front and in the power of a man toward whom he now admitted he'd been in the wrong, kept his eyes fixed on the colonel's athletic back, his light-haired nape, and his red neck. It struck Rostov that Bogdanich was only pretending not to notice him, and that his real purpose was to test the cadet's courage. So he straightened up and looked around cheerfully. Then it seemed to him that Bogdanich was riding so close on purpose, to show off his own bravery. Next he imagined that the colonel would send the squadron on some desperate charge just to punish him—Rostov. And then he pictured how, after the charge, Bogdanich would approach him as he lay wounded and magnanimously extend the hand of reconciliation.

The high-shouldered figure of Zherkov, familiar to the Pavlograds since he'd only recently left their regiment, rode up to the colonel. After being removed from headquarters, Zherkov hadn't stayed with the regiment, claiming he wasn't fool enough to toil at the front when he could earn more rewards by doing nothing on the staff. He had managed to attach himself as an orderly officer to Prince Bagration. Now he came to his former commander with an order from the rear guard.
"Colonel," he said, addressing Rostov's enemy with an air of solemn gravity, glancing around at his former comrades, "there's an order to halt and set fire to the bridge."
"An order from whom?" the colonel asked sourly.
"I don't exactly know 'from whom,'" the cornet replied in a serious tone, "but the prince told me: 'Go and tell the colonel that the hussars must return at once and burn the bridge.'"

Behind Zherkov came another officer from the suite, riding up to the hussar colonel with the same order. After him, the stout Nesvitski came galloping up on a Cossack horse that could barely carry his weight.

"Colonel, what's going on?" he shouted as he approached. "I told you to set fire to the bridge, and now someone's gone and botched it. Everyone over there is in a panic and nobody can figure out what's happening."
The colonel deliberately halted the regiment and turned to Nesvitski.
"You spoke to me about inflammable material," he said, "but you said nothing about setting fire to it."

"But my dear sir," said Nesvitski, reining in and taking off his cap to smooth his sweat-dampened hair with his plump hand, "wasn't I telling you to burn the bridge after the inflammable material had been placed?"

"I am not your 'dear sir,' Mister Staff Officer, and you did not tell me to burn the bridge! I know my duty, and I make it my habit to follow orders strictly. You said the bridge would be burned—but who was supposed to burn it? I couldn't know that by divine inspiration!"
"It's always the same!" Nesvitski said with a wave of his hand. "How did you end up here?" he asked, turning to Zherkov.
"Same errand. But you're soaking wet! Let me wring you out!"
"You were saying, Mister Staff Officer..." the colonel continued in an offended tone.
"Colonel," the officer from the suite cut in, "you need to move quickly, or the enemy will bring up their guns for grapeshot."
The colonel looked silently at the suite officer, then at the stout staff officer, then at Zherkov, and he frowned.
"I vill ze bridge fire," he announced in a solemn tone, as if to declare that despite all the aggravation he was enduring, he would still do the right thing.

Striking his horse with his long, muscular legs as though the animal were to blame for everything, the colonel rode forward and ordered Denisov's squadron—the second, in which Rostov was serving—to return to the bridge.
"There it is—just as I thought," Rostov said to himself. "He wants to test me!" His heart clenched and the blood rushed to his face. "Let him see whether I'm a coward!" he thought.

Once again, the grave expression the men had worn under fire settled over every bright face in the squadron. Rostov kept watching his enemy, the colonel, closely, searching his face for confirmation of his suspicions. But the colonel never once glanced at Rostov and looked just as he always did at the front—solemn and stern. Then came the word of command.
"Quick! Quick!" several voices repeated around him.

Sabers catching on bridles and spurs jingling, the hussars hastily dismounted, none of them quite sure what they were supposed to do. The men were crossing themselves. Rostov no longer looked at the colonel—there was no time. He was terrified of falling behind the others, so terrified that his heart seemed to stop. His hand shook as he handed his horse off to an orderly, and he felt the blood pound against his chest. Denisov rode past him, leaning back and shouting something. Rostov saw nothing but hussars running all around him, their spurs catching and sabers clanking.
"Stretchers!" someone shouted behind him.

Rostov didn't stop to think about what that call meant. He just ran, trying to stay ahead of everyone. But right at the bridge, not watching his feet, he stepped into some sticky, trampled mud, stumbled, and fell on his hands. The others rushed past him.
"At both sides, Captain," he heard the colonel's voice. Bogdanich had ridden ahead and pulled up his horse near the bridge, his face triumphant and cheerful.

Rostov wiped his muddy hands on his trousers, looked at his enemy, and was about to run forward again, thinking the further ahead he got, the better. But Bogdanich, without looking at him or showing any sign of recognition, shouted:
"Who's running down the middle of the bridge? To the right! Come back, Cadet!" he shouted angrily. Then, turning to Denisov, who had ridden out onto the bridge planks to show off his courage:
"Why take unnecessary risks, Captain? You should dismount," he said.
"Every bullet has its target," Vaska Denisov replied, turning in his saddle.

Meanwhile, Nesvitski, Zherkov, and the officer from the suite stood together out of range, watching—now the small cluster of men in yellow shakos, dark-green braided jackets, and blue riding trousers swarming around the bridge, and now what was approaching from the far side: blue uniforms and groups of men with horses, clearly recognizable as artillery.

"Will they manage to burn the bridge or not? Who'll get there first? Will they set it ablaze, or will the French get close enough for grapeshot and wipe them out?" Every man watching from the high ground above the bridge was asking himself these questions with a sinking heart, gazing at the bridge and the hussars in the bright evening light and the blue-coated troops advancing from the other side with bayonets and guns.
"The hussars are going to catch it!" Nesvitski said. "They're within grapeshot range now."
"He shouldn't have taken so many men," the officer from the suite remarked.
"That's true enough," Nesvitski agreed. "Two quick fellows could have done the job just as well."

"Ah, your excellency," Zherkov put in, his eyes fixed on the hussars but still wearing that guileless look that made it impossible to tell whether he was joking or serious. "How you look at things! Send two men? But then who would earn the Vladimir medal and ribbon? As it is, even if they do get peppered, the squadron can be put up for honors and he can win a ribbon. Our Bogdanich knows how things are done."
"There!" said the officer from the suite. "That's grapeshot."
He pointed to the French guns, whose limbers were being hurriedly detached and pulled away.

On the French side, a cloud of smoke rose from one of the gun positions, then a second and a third almost simultaneously. At the moment the first report reached them, a fourth flash was visible. Then two booms in quick succession, and a third.
"Oh! Oh!" Nesvitski groaned as if in sharp pain, grabbing the officer from the suite by the arm. "Look! A man's gone down! Down, down!"
"Two, I think."
"If I were Tsar, I would never go to war," Nesvitski said, turning away.

The French guns were hastily reloaded. The infantry in blue advanced toward the bridge at a run. Smoke appeared again in irregular bursts, and grapeshot crackled and rattled against the bridge. But this time Nesvitski couldn't see what was happening there—a dense cloud of smoke had risen from the bridge. The hussars had managed to set it on fire, and the French batteries were now shooting at them not to stop them, but simply because the guns were aimed and there were targets to hit.

The French managed to fire three rounds of grapeshot before the hussars made it back to their horses. Two of the rounds went wide, the shot sailing too high, but the last one landed in the middle of a cluster of hussars and knocked three of them down.

Rostov, preoccupied with his feelings about Bogdanich, had stopped on the bridge with no idea what to do. There was no one to cut down—he had always imagined battles with saber in hand—and he couldn't help burn the bridge since he hadn't brought any burning straw like the other soldiers. He just stood there looking around, when suddenly he heard a rattling sound on the bridge, like nuts being spilled, and the hussar nearest to him fell against the railing with a groan. Rostov rushed over with the others. Again someone shouted, "Stretchers!" Four men grabbed the hussar and began lifting him.
"Oh God! For Christ's sake, leave me alone!" the wounded man cried, but they lifted him anyway and placed him on the stretcher.

Nikolai Rostov turned away and gazed into the distance, as if searching for something—at the waters of the Danube, at the sky, at the sun. How beautiful the sky was: how blue, how calm, how deep! How bright and glorious the setting sun! How softly the distant waters of the Danube glittered! And more beautiful still were the far-off blue mountains beyond the river, the convent, the mysterious gorges, the pine forests veiled in mist at their summits... There was peace there, and happiness... "I would want nothing else, nothing at all, if only I were there," Rostov thought. "In me alone and in that sunshine there is so much happiness. But here... groans, suffering, fear, and this chaos and rush... Over there—they're shouting again, and again everyone is running somewhere, and I'll run with them, and it—death—is here, above me and all around me... One more instant, and I will never again see this sun, this water, that gorge!..."

At that moment the sun began to slip behind the clouds, and more stretchers came into view before Rostov. And the fear of death and of the stretchers, and the love of the sun and of life, all merged into a single feeling of nauseating dread.
"Oh Lord God! You who are in that heaven—save me, forgive me, and protect me!" Rostov whispered.
The hussars ran back to the men holding their horses. Their voices grew louder and calmer. The stretchers disappeared from sight.
"Well, fwiend? So you've had a taste of gunpowder!" Vaska Denisov shouted right above his ear.
"It's all over—but I'm a coward. Yes, a coward!" Rostov thought, and with a deep sigh he took Rook from the orderly—the horse was standing with one hoof resting—and began to mount.
"Was that grapeshot?" he asked Denisov.

"You bet it was!" Denisov cried. "You all worked like real heroes, and it's nasty business! A charge is good work—hacking away at the enemy! But this kind of thing is pure hell, with them shooting at you like you're a target."
Denisov rode up to a group that had gathered near Rostov, made up of the colonel, Nesvitski, Zherkov, and the officer from the suite.
"Well, it seems no one noticed," Rostov thought. And it was true. No one had paid any attention, because everyone understood the sensation that a cadet experiences under fire for the first time.
"Here's something for you to report," said Zherkov. "Watch—I'll get promoted to sub-lieutenant for this."
"Inform ze prince zat I ze bridge fired!" the colonel declared, triumphant and beaming.
"And if he asks about the losses?"

"A trifle," the colonel said in his deep bass voice. "Two hussars wounded, and one knocked out." He couldn't hold back a satisfied smile, and he pronounced the words "knocked out" with ringing clarity.

chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter IX
paragraphs: Pursued by a French army of a hundred thousand men under Bonaparte's command, met by a hostile local population, losing faith in its allies, short of supplies, and forced to operate under conditions of war that no one had anticipated, the Russian army of thirty-five thousand under Kutuzov was retreating rapidly along the Danube. It halted when overtaken by the enemy and fought rearguard actions only as far as necessary to continue its retreat without losing its heavy equipment. There had been engagements at Lambach, Amstetten, and Melk, but despite the courage and endurance with which the Russians fought—acknowledged even by the enemy—the only result of these battles was an even faster retreat. The Austrian troops that had escaped capture at Ulm and joined Kutuzov at Braunau now broke away from the Russian army, leaving Kutuzov with nothing but his own weak and exhausted forces. The defense of Vienna was no longer thinkable. Instead of the offensive campaign whose plan, carefully devised according to the modern science of strategy, had been handed to Kutuzov in Vienna by the Austrian War Council, his sole remaining objective—and a nearly unattainable one—was to link up with the reinforcements marching from Russia without losing his army the way Mack had lost his at Ulm.

On October 28, Kutuzov crossed with his army to the left bank of the Danube and took up a position for the first time with the river between himself and the bulk of the French forces. On the thirtieth, he attacked Mortier's division on the left bank and shattered it. In this engagement, trophies were captured for the first time: banners, cannons, and two enemy generals. For the first time after two weeks of retreat, Russian troops had halted and, after a fight, had not only held the field but driven the French back. Though the troops were poorly clothed, exhausted, and had lost a third of their strength to dead, wounded, sick, and stragglers—though many of the sick and wounded had been left behind on the far side of the Danube with a letter entrusting them to the enemy's mercy—and though the large hospitals and houses in Krems that had been converted into military hospitals could no longer hold all the casualties—the stand at Krems and the victory over Mortier lifted the army's spirits considerably. Throughout the entire army and at headquarters, the most optimistic (though inaccurate) rumors were circulating: that Russian reinforcement columns were approaching, that the Austrians had won some victory, and that a frightened Bonaparte was in retreat.

Prince Andrei had served during the battle as aide to the Austrian General Schmidt, who was killed in the action. His horse had been shot from under him and a bullet had grazed his arm. As a mark of the commander in chief's special favor, he was chosen to carry the news of this victory to the Austrian court, which was now at Brünn rather than Vienna, since Vienna was threatened by the French. Despite his seemingly delicate build, Prince Andrei could endure physical hardship far better than many much stronger men. On the night of the battle, having arrived at Krems excited but not tired, with dispatches from Dokhturov for Kutuzov, he was immediately sent on with a special dispatch to Brünn. Being chosen for such a mission meant not only a reward but an important step toward promotion.

The night was dark but starry. The road showed black against the snow that had fallen the day before—the day of the battle. Replaying his impressions of the recent fight, pleasantly imagining the reaction his news of victory would produce, remembering the send-off from the commander in chief and his fellow officers, Prince Andrei raced along in a post chaise, savoring the feelings of a man who has finally begun to achieve a long-desired happiness. As soon as he closed his eyes, his ears filled with the rattle of wheels and the sensation of victory. Then he would start imagining that the Russians were fleeing and that he himself had been killed—but he quickly shook off the vision with a surge of joy, as if discovering all over again that none of it was true, that on the contrary, it was the French who had fled. He recalled every detail of the victory once more, and his own steady courage during the battle, and feeling reassured, he drifted off to sleep... The dark, starry night gave way to a bright, cheerful morning. The snow was melting in the sunshine, the horses galloped briskly, and on both sides of the road stretched forests of different kinds, fields, and villages.

At one of the relay stations he overtook a convoy of Russian wounded. The Russian officer in charge of the transport was sprawled in the front cart, shouting at a soldier with crude abuse. In each of the long German carts, six or more pale, dirty, bandaged men were being jolted over the rough road. Some were talking—he caught Russian words—and others were chewing bread. The more severely wounded watched in silence, with the dull curiosity of sick children, as the courier rushed past them.

Prince Andrei told his driver to stop and asked a soldier which battle they had been wounded in. "Day before yesterday, on the Danube," the soldier answered. Prince Andrei took out his purse and gave the man three gold coins.
"That's for all of them," he said to the officer who came up.
"Get well soon, lads!" he called to the soldiers. "There's still plenty to do."
"Any news, sir?" asked the officer, clearly eager to strike up a conversation.
"Good news! Drive on!" he shouted to his driver, and they galloped away.

It was already quite dark by the time Prince Andrei rattled over the cobblestone streets of Brünn and found himself surrounded by tall buildings, the glow of shop windows and house lamps, elegant carriages, and all the bustle of a large, lively city—always so appealing to a soldier after life in camp. Despite his rapid journey and sleepless night, he felt even more energized and alert as he pulled up to the palace than he had the day before. Only his eyes had a feverish gleam, and his thoughts followed one another with extraordinary speed and clarity. He relived the details of the battle once more—no longer hazy, but sharp and precise, framed in the concise form in which he imagined reporting them to Emperor Francis. He vividly anticipated the offhand questions that might be asked and the answers he would give. He expected to be ushered into the Emperor's presence immediately. At the main entrance to the palace, however, an official hurried out to meet him and, learning that he was a special messenger, directed him to a different entrance.
"To the right down the corridor, Your Excellency! There you'll find the adjutant on duty," the official said. "He will take you to the Minister of War."

The adjutant on duty met Prince Andrei, asked him to wait, and went in to see the minister. Five minutes later he returned and, bowing with exaggerated courtesy, led Prince Andrei along a corridor to the room where the Minister of War was working. The adjutant's elaborate politeness seemed designed to discourage any attempt at familiarity from the Russian messenger.

Prince Andrei's elated mood dimmed considerably as he approached the minister's door. He felt slighted, and without being fully aware of it, his sense of offense immediately hardened into a disdain that was entirely uncalled for. His quick mind instantly supplied a perspective that gave him the right to look down on both the adjutant and the minister. "Far from the smell of gunpowder, they probably think winning victories is easy!" he thought. His eyes narrowed scornfully as he entered the Minister of War's room with deliberately measured steps. This feeling of contempt only deepened when he saw the minister seated at a large table, reading documents and marking them with pencil notes, paying no attention whatsoever to his arrival for the first two or three minutes. A wax candle stood on either side of the minister's bent, bald head with its gray temples. He went on reading to the end without looking up at the sound of the door opening and footsteps approaching.
"Take this and deliver it," he said to his adjutant, handing over the papers and still not acknowledging the special messenger.

Prince Andrei felt that either Kutuzov's army interested the Minister of War less than the other matters on his desk, or the minister wanted to give that impression. "But it makes absolutely no difference to me," he thought. The minister gathered the remaining papers, straightened them into a neat pile, and finally raised his head. He had a distinctive, intelligent face—but the moment he turned to Prince Andrei, its firm, perceptive expression shifted in a way that was clearly deliberate and habitual. His face assumed the stupid, artificial smile—making no attempt whatsoever to disguise its falseness—of a man who spends his days receiving one petitioner after another.
[Speaking in French] "From Field Marshal Kutuzov?" he asked. "Good news, I hope? An engagement with Mortier? A victory? It was about time!"
He took the dispatch addressed to him and began reading it with a sorrowful expression.
"Oh, my God! My God! Schmidt!" he exclaimed in German. "What a catastrophe! What a catastrophe!"
Having skimmed the dispatch, he laid it on the table and studied Prince Andrei, clearly turning something over in his mind.

"What a tragedy! You say the battle was decisive? But Mortier was not captured." He reflected again. "I'm very glad you've brought good news, though Schmidt's death is a heavy price for this victory. His Majesty will certainly want to see you, but not today. I thank you! You need rest. Come to the levee tomorrow, after the parade. I'll send word, however."
The stupid smile, which had vanished while he was speaking, reappeared on his face.
[Speaking in French] "Goodbye! Thank you very much. His Majesty will most likely wish to see you," he added with a bow.

When Prince Andrei left the palace, he felt that all the excitement and happiness the victory had given him had been surrendered into the indifferent hands of the Minister of War and the polite adjutant. The entire character of his thoughts changed in an instant; the battle now seemed like the memory of some distant event, long past.
